True.

The chapter states that to ensure free and fair elections in India the Election Commission has adopted several measures, and that the Code of Conduct is one of the measures adopted by the Election Commission. The Code of Conduct explains the rules that are to be followed by the Government, political parties and voters before elections and during elections. The chapter further says that the Government has to observe the code of conduct declared by the Election Commission and that even the Government cannot violate these rules. Laying down the code of conduct is therefore the work of the Election Commission, and its strict observance in the last few elections has made the common voters confident.

True.

Resolving any disputes relating to elections is one of the functions of the Election Commission listed in the chapter. The chapter says that the Election Commission has the responsibility of resolving any disputes that may arise regarding elections, and that accordingly, to declare any candidate as disqualified or to conduct re-election in a particular constituency is the responsibility of the Election Commission. So when such a special situation arises, the Election Commission can order the election in that constituency to be held again.

False.

Deciding the timetable and the programme of elections is listed in the chapter as a function of the Election Commission, not of the state government. The chapter states that the conduct of elections is entirely the responsibility of the Election Commission, and that the Election Commission decides when to conduct elections and in how many stages to hold elections in every state. The Constitution of India has made provision for an independent Election Commission precisely so that the election process is free, fair and reliable; if a state government fixed its own election timetable, that independence would be lost.

Every member of the Loksabha represents one constituency. The total number of members in the Loksabha is 543, which means there are 543 constituencies of the Loksabha. Reorganising or restructuring the constituencies means redrawing these constituencies. The chapter states that creating constituencies is the responsibility of the Delimitation Commission, and that the Delimitation Commission does not succumb to any pressure while restructuring the constituencies. Because the work is done without yielding to pressure, the constituencies are formed impartially, which helps keep the electoral process fair.

[Note: the chapter does not state on what basis constituencies are reorganised or how often the reorganisation is carried out. The chapter's prose calls the body responsible the Delimitation Commission, while the exercise describes it as the Delimitation committee of the Election Commission.]

Loksabha elections held after every five years are called general elections. Sometimes, however, elections have to be held before that term is complete. If the elected government loses its majority before completing its term in the Parliament, or if the parties of the coalition government withdraw their support resulting in the loss of majority support for the government, and if no alternative government is possible, then elections are held before the completion of the term. Such elections held before the government completes its full term are called midterm elections.

Centre : The process of elections

| Branch | Point to be filled in |
|---|---|
| Role of the Election Commission | Prepares and updates the voters list, includes the names of new voters and issues identity cards to voters. |
| Role of the Election Commission | Decides the timetable and the programme of elections, that is, when the elections are to be held and in how many stages they will be held in every state. |
| Role of the Election Commission | Scrutinises the applications of candidates, gives recognition to political parties and allots them election symbols, resolves disputes regarding elections and lays down the code of conduct. |
| Role of the voters | Gets his or her name entered in the voters list; every Indian citizen who has completed 18 years of age has a right to vote, and the name must be in the voters list to exercise that right. |
| Role of the voters | Casts the vote, because the chapter says voting is our duty as well as a responsibility; if the voter does not want to vote for any candidate, the option of 'None of the above' (NOTA) can be chosen. |
| Role of the voters | Follows the code of conduct, since the code explains the rules that are to be followed by voters before elections and during elections. |
| Role of political parties and their candidates | Select the candidates who will contest the elections and fill in the application forms giving information about themselves, which the Election Commission then scrutinises; the parties also get themselves recognised by the Election Commission and receive an election symbol. |
| Role of political parties and their candidates | Carry out the election campaign while obeying the code of conduct, keep their official representatives present at the time of voting and counting of votes, and help the Election Commission to control violence during elections. |

The chapter lists five functions of the Election Commission.

1. Preparing the voters list : Every Indian citizen who has completed 18 years of age has a right to vote, but to exercise it the citizen's name must be in the voters list. It is the responsibility of the Election Commission to prepare the list of eligible voters, update the existing voters list and include the names of new voters. The Commission also has the authority to issue identity cards to the voters.

2. Decide the timetable and the programme of elections : The conduct of elections is entirely the responsibility of the Election Commission. It decides when to conduct elections and in how many stages to hold elections in every state.

3. Scrutiny of the applications of candidates : After the election dates are declared, political parties select their candidates and some candidates contest independently. All of them have to fill applications giving information about themselves. The Election Commission scrutinises all the applications and allows the eligible candidates to contest.

4. Give recognition to political parties : All political parties are required to be recognised by the Election Commission, and the Commission also has the right to derecognise any political party. It allots election symbols to the political parties.

5. To resolve any disputes relating to elections : The Election Commission has the responsibility of resolving any disputes that arise regarding elections. Accordingly, declaring a candidate disqualified or conducting a re-election in a particular constituency is its responsibility.

Art. 324 of the Indian Constitution has established the Election Commission as an autonomous body. It consists of one Chief Election Commissioner and two other commissioners. The President appoints the election commissioners. The Chief Election Commissioner cannot be removed from his post easily or on account of any political reasons, and the chapter says this is necessary so as to preserve the independence of the Election Commission. A separate provision is also made for the expenses of the Election Commission. The Election Commission does not have a separate staff of its own; government officers, teachers and other employees help the Commission to execute the process of elections. Sukumar Sen was the first Chief Election Commissioner after independence, and he was given charge after the Election Commission was established in 1950.

[Note: the chapter does not state the term or tenure of the post of Election Commissioner, nor the procedure by which the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed.]

To ensure free and fair elections in India, the Election Commission has adopted several measures, and the Code of Conduct is one of them. The Code of Conduct explains the rules that are to be followed by the Government, political parties and voters before elections and during elections. Even the Government cannot violate these rules. In the last few decades the Election Commission has used its powers through such measures to control malpractices during elections, and the chapter asks students to identify violations of the code from examples such as a candidate distributing items of household use or appealing for support on the basis of caste and religion. Because the code of conduct has been strictly observed in the last few elections, the common voters have become confident about the electoral process.
